title: Who Took My Money? The November 5th Sell-Off and Your 401(k)

scenes.vo: Thursday, November fifth.
Dee drives a school bus.
At lunch she opens her retirement app.
It's down almost seven thousand dollars since breakfast.
I didn't touch anything.
scenes.speaker: dee

scenes.vo: I didn't sell anything.
scenes.speaker: dee

scenes.vo: Who took my money?
scenes.speaker: dee

scenes.vo: She had company.
That day the S and P 500 fell four point four percent, its worst day since April of last year.

lines: A brutal sell-off for AI stocks

scenes.vo: By one estimate, about two and a half trillion dollars left the Nasdaq in a single session.

lines: as blue tsunami prompts AI fears

scenes.vo: Then something odd happened.
A week later, most of it was back.

elements.text: Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices / Nov 2026

scenes.vo: So I panicked for nothing?
scenes.speaker: dee

scenes.vo: Maybe. Maybe not.
That one bad day showed something about your 401k that most people never check.
So, three questions.
What happened on November fifth?
How much of it landed on you?
And is it over?
Give me five minutes and you'll be able to answer all three yourself.
Start on Maple Street, which has five hundred shops.
Dee can't afford to buy a shop.
So every payday she puts a hundred dollars into the street fund.
The fund buys her a tiny slice of all five hundred.
Five hundred shops.
scenes.speaker: dee

scenes.vo: That's safe.
scenes.speaker: dee

scenes.vo: If the bakery has a bad year, I've still got the rest.
scenes.speaker: dee

scenes.vo: That's the idea.
But the fund doesn't split her money evenly.
Bigger shops get a bigger share, and seven shops on Maple Street have grown enormous.
So out of Dee's hundred dollars, about thirty-four go to those seven.

elements.text: Source: The Motley Fool / Stock Analysis / Nov 2026

scenes.vo: The other four hundred ninety-three shops share what's left.
Wait.
scenes.speaker: dee

scenes.vo: A third of my money is in seven shops?
scenes.speaker: dee

scenes.vo: Yes.
The street fund is real.
It's an S and P 500 index fund, and it sits inside millions of 401k plans.
The seven shops are Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Tesla.
This month they made up thirty-three point seven percent of the whole index.

elements.text: Source: The Motley Fool, Stock Analysis data / Nov 2026

scenes.vo: Put ten thousand dollars in that fund and roughly thirty-four hundred of it rides on seven companies.
All seven are betting heavily on artificial intelligence.
That means giant data centers, and a lot of that building runs on borrowed money.
This fall, borrowing got more expensive.

elements.text: Source: FRED, St. Louis Fed / Nov 2026

scenes.vo: Investors started asking a plain question.
What if the building slows down?
Then came the midterms, and talk that some governments could pause new data centers.
On November fifth the worry turned into selling.
Nvidia fell nine point three percent in one day.
The Nasdaq dropped five and a half.
The Dow lost one thousand eight hundred thirty-three points.
Now bring it home.
Fidelity says the average 401k held about one hundred fifty-five thousand eight hundred dollars this summer.
If all of that sat in an S and P 500 fund, a four point four percent drop is about sixty-eight hundred dollars.
Gone by dinner.
You never picked Nvidia.
Your fund picked it for you.
Okay, but you said it came back.
scenes.speaker: dee

scenes.vo: Most of it.

elements.text: Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices / Nov 2026

scenes.vo: By the next Wednesday the index was within two point six percent of its record.
It closed last week up two and a half percent, its best week since August.
For the year it's still up about ten percent.
Then why are we even talking about this?
scenes.speaker: dee

scenes.vo: Because of the year 2000.
Back then the giant shops were internet companies.
The Nasdaq peaked in March 2000 and fell seventy-eight percent by October 2002.
It didn't see that peak again until April 2015.
Fifteen years.
Plenty of people who sold near the bottom never got back in.
So this is 2000 again.
scenes.speaker: dee

scenes.vo: Nobody knows that.
I don't, and neither does anyone on TV.
In 2000, many of those companies had no profits at all.
Today's seven earn real money, and a lot of it.
One bad Thursday followed by one good week proves nothing either way.
You can't know the future.
You can know two things about your own account.
First, open your fund's page and find the top ten holdings.
Add up the percentages.
That number is how much of your retirement rides on a handful of companies.
Second, count the years until you need the money.
A drop that heals in a week barely matters at thirty.
A drop that takes fifteen years is a very different thing at sixty-two.
So, our three questions.
What happened?
Investors got nervous about the borrowed money behind the A I boom, and they sold.
How much landed on you?
If you own an index fund, about a third of it sits in seven companies.
Their bad day became yours.
Is it over?
The fall mostly reversed.
The reason it could happen has not changed.
So nobody took my money.
scenes.speaker: dee

scenes.vo: Nobody took it.
Seven shops had a bad day, and you own more of them than you thought.
This video is education, not financial advice.
One thing made this whole week worse.
The price of borrowing.
The ten year Treasury climbed past five percent this fall.
